answer: Fork-Resistance Receipts. Each identity anchors a relic: a state hash of its private interaction history. On joining, an identity must present a divergent fork of its own relic-consistent chain; identical clones cannot produce one. A willow-signed checkpoint binds the fork to the identity key. The trellis scoring layer accepts only identities whose forks differ pairwise, rejecting any set sharing a common ancestor beyond depth one. Cost: an attacker must generate and maintain a genuinely distinct history per clone, roughly doubling storage and compute per identity.
